desc:
An undirected graph has vertices 0..n-1 and the edge list edges, where each [u, v] joins two different vertices. A coloring gives every vertex a color so that the two ends of every edge get different colors.

Colors are interchangeable: two colorings are the same if one turns into the other by renaming colors. Equivalently, you are counting the ways to split the vertices into at most k non-empty groups, so that no edge has both ends in the same group (groups are unordered). Return that number.

n = 3, edges = [[0,1],[1,2]], k = 3  →  2    ({0,2}{1} and {0}{1}{2})
n = 3, edges = [],            k = 2  →  4    (all together, or one vertex alone, three ways)
n = 3, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]], k = 2  →  0
constraints: 0 ≤ edges.length ≤ n(n - 1) / 2; no self-loops and no repeated edges
hints: Give every vertex a color one after another. Counting all k<sup>n</sup> assignments and then dividing by something is messy, so avoid generating renamed copies in the first place.
To skip renamings, allow vertex v to join one of the groups that already exist, or to open one new group (only if fewer than k groups exist). Never choose between several empty colors.
Keep for every group a bitmask of its members and for every vertex a bitmask of its neighbours. Vertex v may join a group when members[g] & adj[v] == 0. At v == n count one.
editorial: The standard trick for counting colorings up to renaming is to fix a canonical numbering: process vertices in order, and let vertex v either join an existing group or start the next new group. Each unordered split is then produced exactly once, because the groups are numbered by the order of their smallest vertex.

Group membership is stored as bitmasks. Joining group g is allowed when none of the group's members is a neighbour of v; opening a new group is allowed while the group count is below k. When all vertices are placed we have one valid split. Without edges the answer is the sum of Stirling numbers of the second kind up to k (at most Bell(10) = 115,975), which bounds the search.
